claim: Preterm infants are susceptible to neonatal sepsis, a syndrome of pro-inflammatory activity, organ damage, and altered metabolism following infection.
source: Preterm infants are susceptible to neonatal sepsis, a syndrome of pro-inflammatory activity, organ damage, and altered metabolism following infection.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about preterm infants and neonatal sepsis that is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: A reduced glucose regime during infection increased survival in preterm pigs.
source: We found that a reduced glucose regime during infection increased survival via reduced pro-inflammatory response, while maintaining normoglycemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A reduced glucose regime during infection reduced pro-inflammatory response in preterm pigs.
source: We found that a reduced glucose regime during infection increased survival via reduced pro-inflammatory response, while maintaining normoglycemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1I-K.

claim: A reduced glucose regime during infection maintained normoglycemia in preterm pigs.
source: We found that a reduced glucose regime during infection increased survival via reduced pro-inflammatory response, while maintaining normoglycemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Reduced glucose intervention enhanced hepatic oxidative phosphorylation in infected preterm pigs.
source: Mechanistically, this intervention enhanced hepatic oxidative phosphorylation and possibly gluconeogenesis, and dampened both circulating and hepatic inflammation.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Reduced glucose intervention possibly enhanced hepatic gluconeogenesis in infected preterm pigs.
source: Mechanistically, this intervention enhanced hepatic oxidative phosphorylation and possibly gluconeogenesis, and dampened both circulating and hepatic inflammation.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative finding based on transcriptomic and metabolomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Reduced glucose intervention dampened circulating inflammation in infected preterm pigs.
source: Mechanistically, this intervention enhanced hepatic oxidative phosphorylation and possibly gluconeogenesis, and dampened both circulating and hepatic inflammation.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by plasma cytokine data shown in Figures 1I-K.

claim: Reduced glucose intervention dampened hepatic inflammation in infected preterm pigs.
source: Mechanistically, this intervention enhanced hepatic oxidative phosphorylation and possibly gluconeogenesis, and dampened both circulating and hepatic inflammation.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by hepatic transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Switching from a high to a reduced glucose supply after the debut of clinical symptoms did not prevent sepsis in preterm pigs.
source: However, switching from a high to a reduced glucose supply after the debut of clinical symptoms did not prevent sepsis, suggesting metabolic conditions at the start of infection are key in driving the outcome.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Metabolic conditions at the start of infection are key in driving the outcome of sepsis in preterm pigs.
source: However, switching from a high to a reduced glucose supply after the debut of clinical symptoms did not prevent sepsis, suggesting metabolic conditions at the start of infection are key in driving the outcome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Early therapy with purified human inter-alpha inhibitor protein partially reversed the effects of low parenteral glucose provision in infected preterm pigs.
source: Finally, an early therapy with purified human inter-alpha inhibitor protein, a liver-derived anti-inflammatory protein, partially reversed the effects of low parenteral glucose provision, likely by inhibiting neutrophil functions that mediate pathogen clearance.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Human inter-alpha inhibitor protein likely inhibits neutrophil functions that mediate pathogen clearance.
source: Finally, an early therapy with purified human inter-alpha inhibitor protein, a liver-derived anti-inflammatory protein, partially reversed the effects of low parenteral glucose provision, likely by inhibiting neutrophil functions that mediate pathogen clearance.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 7H-I.

claim: Most episodes of late-onset sepsis in preterm infants are caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci.
source: Most episodes of late-onset sepsis in these infants (occurring >48 hr after birth) are caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (CONS), such as Staphylococcus epidermidis (Strunk et al., 2021; Shane et al., 2017), which may enter the circulation via indwelling medical devices or from the gastrointestinal tract (Deitch, 2012; Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Coagulase-negative staphylococci may enter the circulation via indwelling medical devices or from the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Most episodes of late-onset sepsis in these infants (occurring >48 hr after birth) are caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (CONS), such as Staphylococcus epidermidis (Strunk et al., 2021; Shane et al., 2017), which may enter the circulation via indwelling medical devices or from the gastrointestinal tract (Deitch, 2012; Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Immune cells in healthy adults undergo a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis upon exogenous challenge.
source: Upon exogenous challenge, immune cells and many other cell types in healthy adults undergo a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to glycolysis, producing large amounts of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to fuel inflammatory responses, facilitating efficient reduction of pathogen burden through immunological resistance (Harbeson et al., 2018; Gaber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis produces large amounts of ATP to fuel inflammatory responses.
source: Upon exogenous challenge, immune cells and many other cell types in healthy adults undergo a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to glycolysis, producing large amounts of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to fuel inflammatory responses, facilitating efficient reduction of pathogen burden through immunological resistance (Harbeson et al., 2018; Gaber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Immune cells can employ a tolerance strategy by shifting from glycolysis to OXPHOS.
source: However, immune cells can also employ a tolerance strategy, limiting the active resistance response and associated immunopathology, via an opposite shift from glycolysis to OXPHOS (Harbeson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Newborns, especially those born prematurely, display low immune cell metabolism.
source: Therefore, energy tends to be prioritized for vital organ functions rather than immune responses to external stimuli, explaining why they display low immune cell metabolism (Harbeson et al., 2018; Kollmann et al., 2012) and can withstand 10–100 times greater pathogen loads than adults before showing clinical symptoms (Strnad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Newborns can withstand 10–100 times greater pathogen loads than adults before showing clinical symptoms.
source: Therefore, energy tends to be prioritized for vital organ functions rather than immune responses to external stimuli, explaining why they display low immune cell metabolism (Harbeson et al., 2018; Kollmann et al., 2012) and can withstand 10–100 times greater pathogen loads than adults before showing clinical symptoms (Strnad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking hepatic glycolysis lowers overall energy expenditure and improves OXPHOS in mice.
source: For instance, blocking hepatic glycolysis lowers overall energy expenditure and improves OXPHOS, which facilitates immune tolerance and better survival during polymicrobial sepsis in mice (Mainali et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking hepatic glycolysis facilitates immune tolerance and better survival during polymicrobial sepsis in mice.
source: For instance, blocking hepatic glycolysis lowers overall energy expenditure and improves OXPHOS, which facilitates immune tolerance and better survival during polymicrobial sepsis in mice (Mainali et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Components of Inter-Alpha Inhibitor Protein are differentially regulated during sepsis leading to a significant reduction of the whole complex in adults.
source: Recent studies have shown that the components of one of the most abundant plasma protein complexes, Inter-Alpha Inhibitor Protein (IAIP), are differentially regulated during sepsis leading to a significant reduction of the whole complex both in adults (Lim et al., 2003; Opal et al., 2007; Rucevic et al., 2007) and neonates (Baek et al., 2003; Chaaban et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Components of Inter-Alpha Inhibitor Protein are differentially regulated during sepsis leading to a significant reduction of the whole complex in neonates.
source: Recent studies have shown that the components of one of the most abundant plasma protein complexes, Inter-Alpha Inhibitor Protein (IAIP), are differentially regulated during sepsis leading to a significant reduction of the whole complex both in adults (Lim et al., 2003; Opal et al., 2007; Rucevic et al., 2007) and neonates (Baek et al., 2003; Chaaban et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Administration of enriched human plasma-derived IAIP in a murine model of neonatal sepsis reduces disease severity and mortality through suppression of pro-inflammatory responses.
source: Administration of enriched human plasma-derived IAIP (hIAIP) in a murine model of neonatal sepsis has been shown to reduce disease severity and mortality through suppression of pro-inflammatory responses (Singh et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Hyperglycemia occurs in up to 80% of very preterm infants during early life.
source: However, this practice leads to hyperglycemia in up to 80% of very preterm infants during early life (Beardsall et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Prolonged glucose-rich PN is related to longer hospitalization in septic infants.
source: Prolonged glucose-rich PN is related to longer hospitalization in septic infants (Alaedeen et al., 2006), which suggests it may affect the blood immune-metabolic axis or hepatic metabolism during infection, facilitating glycolysis and active immune resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Limited nutrition in the acute phase of bacterial infection in rodents reduced glycolysis and enhanced disease tolerance, leading to better survival.
source: This is in line with a recent study showing that limited nutrition in the acute phase of bacterial infection in rodents reduced glycolysis and enhanced disease tolerance, leading to better survival (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Preterm pigs mimic clinical and cellular infection responses to S. epidermidis as seen in septic preterm infants.
source: Preterm pigs provide a unique, prematurely born, animal model, enabling PN via an umbilical catheter and mimicking clinical and cellular infection responses to S. epidermidis (Bæk et al., 2020b; Brunse et al., 2018), as seen in septic preterm infants similarly infected with CONS (Strunk et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High parenteral glucose supply exaggerated systemic glycolysis in preterm pigs.
source: With this model, we have previously shown that the high parenteral glucose supply used in neonatal intensive care units exaggerated systemic glycolysis, triggering hyper-inflammatory responses and clinical sepsis signs, whereas strict glucose restriction prevented sepsis, but caused hypoglycemia (Muk et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: High parenteral glucose supply triggered hyper-inflammatory responses and clinical sepsis signs in preterm pigs.
source: With this model, we have previously shown that the high parenteral glucose supply used in neonatal intensive care units exaggerated systemic glycolysis, triggering hyper-inflammatory responses and clinical sepsis signs, whereas strict glucose restriction prevented sepsis, but caused hypoglycemia (Muk et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Reduced glucose supply markedly improved survival following infection in preterm pigs, with an almost six-fold reduction in the absolute risk of death.
source: Reduced glucose supply markedly improved survival following infection, with an almost six-fold reduction in the absolute risk of death (p<0.001, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance.

claim: Blood glucose levels remained stable around 2–3 mmol/l during the whole experiment in SE-Low animals.
source: The reduced glucose supply expectedly led to lower blood glucose levels, compared to SE-High animals, and blood glucose levels remained stable around 2–3 mmol/l during the whole experiment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Blood pH started to decrease at a slower rate from 6 hr onwards in SE-Low animals.
source: Blood pH started to decrease at a slower rate from 6 hr onwards in SE-Low animals with correspondingly lower lactate levels, indicating slower rates of glycolytic breakdown of pyruvate (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood gas data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SE-Low animals had lower lactate levels, indicating slower rates of glycolytic breakdown of pyruvate.
source: Blood pH started to decrease at a slower rate from 6 hr onwards in SE-Low animals with correspondingly lower lactate levels, indicating slower rates of glycolytic breakdown of pyruvate (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood lactate data shown in Figure 1E, with an inference about glycolytic breakdown.

claim: Base excess was improved in SE-Low animals already from 3 hr after the start of the infection.
source: Of note, base excess was improved in SE-Low animals already from 3 hr after the start of the infection, whereas glucose supply during infection had no impact on partial carbon dioxide pressure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood gas data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Glucose supply during infection had no impact on partial carbon dioxide pressure.
source: Of note, base excess was improved in SE-Low animals already from 3 hr after the start of the infection, whereas glucose supply during infection had no impact on partial carbon dioxide pressure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood gas data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The severity of the metabolic acidosis occurring during neonatal sepsis was alleviated by the reduced glucose regimen.
source: This indicates that the severity of the metabolic acidosis occurring during neonatal sepsis was alleviated by the reduced glucose regimen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the blood gas data presented in Figures 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blood osmolality did not differ much among the groups.
source: Importantly, despite the marked difference in blood glucose levels, blood osmolality did not differ much among the groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), underlining that the differences in clinical responses were not driven by a hyperosmolar state induced by the high glucose supply.
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood osmolality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The differences in clinical responses were not driven by a hyperosmolar state induced by the high glucose supply.
source: Importantly, despite the marked difference in blood glucose levels, blood osmolality did not differ much among the groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), underlining that the differences in clinical responses were not driven by a hyperosmolar state induced by the high glucose supply.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the blood osmolality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SE-Low animals showed consistently lower blood bacterial densities for the duration of the experiment.
source: SE-Low animals showed consistently lower blood bacterial densities for the duration of the experiment (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by blood bacterial density data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: All the main blood leucocyte subsets dropped in response to the infection.
source: All the main blood leucocyte subsets dropped in response to the infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), but depletions in circulating neutrophils were more pronounced in SE-High vs. SE-Low animals, evident at 6 h post-infection which were only replenished in SE-Low animals (Figure 1G), suggesting either better bone marrow capacity or less neutrophil activation, although this was not further investigated.
evidence: This is a finding supported by hematology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Depletions in circulating neutrophils were more pronounced in SE-High vs. SE-Low animals, evident at 6 h post-infection.
source: All the main blood leucocyte subsets dropped in response to the infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), but depletions in circulating neutrophils were more pronounced in SE-High vs. SE-Low animals, evident at 6 h post-infection which were only replenished in SE-Low animals (Figure 1G), suggesting either better bone marrow capacity or less neutrophil activation, although this was not further investigated.
evidence: This is a finding supported by neutrophil count data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Circulating neutrophils were only replenished in SE-Low animals.
source: All the main blood leucocyte subsets dropped in response to the infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), but depletions in circulating neutrophils were more pronounced in SE-High vs. SE-Low animals, evident at 6 h post-infection which were only replenished in SE-Low animals (Figure 1G), suggesting either better bone marrow capacity or less neutrophil activation, although this was not further investigated.
evidence: This is a finding supported by neutrophil count data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: SE-Low animals showed less severe thrombocytopenia.
source: Also, SE-Low animals showed less severe thrombocytopenia (Figure 1H), and depletions of these blood cellular subsets are known to be associated with increased severity in neonatal sepsis (Melvan et al., 2010; Panda et al., 2021; Timperi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding supported by platelet count data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Depletions of neutrophils and platelets are known to be associated with increased severity in neonatal sepsis.
source: Also, SE-Low animals showed less severe thrombocytopenia (Figure 1H), and depletions of these blood cellular subsets are known to be associated with increased severity in neonatal sepsis (Melvan et al., 2010; Panda et al., 2021; Timperi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The inflammatory response in infected animals with a reduced glucose supply was dramatically attenuated, with lower levels of plasma TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-10.
source: In parallel, it was evident that the inflammatory response in infected animals with a reduced glucose supply also was dramatically attenuated, with lower levels of plasma TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-10, compared to animals with a high glucose supply (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by plasma cytokine data shown in Figures 1I-K.

claim: Differences in TNF-α and IL-6 levels were already evident at 6 hr after inoculation.
source: Differences in TNF-α and IL-6 levels were already evident at 6 hr after inoculation.
evidence: This is a finding supported by plasma cytokine data shown in Figures 1I-J.

claim: Among uninfected control animals, a reduced glucose supply increased IL-10 levels.
source: Interestingly, among uninfected control animals, a reduced glucose supply also increased IL-10 levels (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by plasma IL-10 data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Within SE-Low and SE-High pigs, mortality did not correlate to bacterial burdens.
source: However, within SE-Low and SE-High pigs, mortality did not correlate to bacterial burdens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both infection and glucose supply dramatically impacted hepatic gene transcription, with more than 4000 differentially expressed genes for each group comparison.
source: Both infection and glucose supply dramatically impacted hepatic gene transcription, with more than 4000 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for each group comparison (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Relative to SE-High, the SE-Low animals showed elevated pathways related to glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, OXPHOS, and TCA cycle.
source: Relative to SE-High, the SE-Low animals showed elevated pathways related to glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, OXPHOS, and TCA cycle, as well as fatty acid and glucogenic amino acid metabolism (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and all DEGs can be found in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of transcriptomic data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SE-Low animals showed elevated pathways related to fatty acid and glucogenic amino acid metabolism.
source: Relative to SE-High, the SE-Low animals showed elevated pathways related to glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, OXPHOS, and TCA cycle, as well as fatty acid and glucogenic amino acid metabolism (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and all DEGs can be found in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enzymes related solely to glycolysis or glycogen formation, such as glucokinase (GCK) and phosphoglucomutase 2 (PGM2) were downregulated in SE-Low compared to SE-High.
source: Though glycolysis and gluconeogenesis share many enzymes catalyzing reversible reactions, enzymes related solely to glycolysis or glycogen formation, such as glucokinase (GCK) and phosphoglucomutase 2 (PGM2) were downregulated in SE-Low compared to SE-High (Figure 3D and E), whereas those only involved in gluconeogenesis, such as fructose-bisphosphatase 2 (FBP2) and pyruvate carboxylase (PC) were upregulated (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Enzymes only involved in gluconeogenesis, such as fructose-bisphosphatase 2 (FBP2) and pyruvate carboxylase (PC) were upregulated in SE-Low compared to SE-High.
source: Though glycolysis and gluconeogenesis share many enzymes catalyzing reversible reactions, enzymes related solely to glycolysis or glycogen formation, such as glucokinase (GCK) and phosphoglucomutase 2 (PGM2) were downregulated in SE-Low compared to SE-High (Figure 3D and E), whereas those only involved in gluconeogenesis, such as fructose-bisphosphatase 2 (FBP2) and pyruvate carboxylase (PC) were upregulated (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: A shift from glycolysis to gluconeogenesis occurs in infected animals kept on a reduced glucose supply.
source: This suggests that a shift from glycolysis to gluconeogenesis occurs in infected animals kept on a reduced glucose supply, even during infections.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data shown in Figures 2D-G.

claim: SE-Low animals showed multiple attenuated pathways related to inflammation, including NF-kappa B, IL-17, TNF, and TGF-β signaling.
source: In parallel, SE-Low animals showed multiple attenuated pathways related to inflammation, including NF-kappa B, IL-17, TNF, and Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the two un-infected control groups, glucose supply affected similar metabolic processes, but not inflammatory pathways.
source: Within the two un-infected control groups, glucose supply affected similar metabolic processes, but not inflammatory pathways.
evidence: This is a finding inferred from the transcriptomic analysis comparing control groups.

claim: The metabolite profile of SE-High animals appeared to be distinct from the remaining three groups.
source: The metabolite profile of SE-High animals appeared to be distinct from the remaining three groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by PCA of metabolomic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Infection changed abundance of 11 and 28 metabolites in reduced and high glucose conditions, respectively.
source: Infection changed abundance of 11 and 28 metabolites in reduced and high glucose conditions, respectively, while 35 metabolites were differentially regulated between the two infected groups (All differentially expressed metabolites shown in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the metabolomic analysis.

claim: 35 metabolites were differentially regulated between the two infected groups.
source: Infection changed abundance of 11 and 28 metabolites in reduced and high glucose conditions, respectively, while 35 metabolites were differentially regulated between the two infected groups (All differentially expressed metabolites shown in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the metabolomic analysis.

claim: SE-High animals showed higher levels of succinate and fumarate.
source: Importantly, SE-High animals showed higher levels of succinate and fumarate (Figure 3H–I), further supporting that high glucose supply rewired systemic metabolism to heightened glycolysis, via inhibiting enzymes catalyzing succinate conversion, causing accumulation of succinate and fumarate (Rosenberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding supported by metabolomic data shown in Figures 3H-I.

claim: High glucose supply rewired systemic metabolism to heightened glycolysis, via inhibiting enzymes catalyzing succinate conversion, causing accumulation of succinate and fumarate.
source: Importantly, SE-High animals showed higher levels of succinate and fumarate (Figure 3H–I), further supporting that high glucose supply rewired systemic metabolism to heightened glycolysis, via inhibiting enzymes catalyzing succinate conversion, causing accumulation of succinate and fumarate (Rosenberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from metabolomic data and supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SE-Low animals showed decreased plasma alanine and alanine aminotransferase activity.
source: On the other hand, SE-Low animals showed decreased plasma alanine and alanine aminotransferase activity, and increased levels of blood urea nitrogen, glutamate, and aspartate (Figure 3E, G, J and L), all pointing to the direction of enhanced gluconeogenesis by metabolizing glucogenic amino acids, possibly contributing to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis under reduced glucose supply.
evidence: This is a finding supported by metabolomic and biochemical data shown in Figures 3E, 3J.

claim: SE-Low animals showed increased levels of blood urea nitrogen, glutamate, and aspartate.
source: On the other hand, SE-Low animals showed decreased plasma alanine and alanine aminotransferase activity, and increased levels of blood urea nitrogen, glutamate, and aspartate (Figure 3E, G, J and L), all pointing to the direction of enhanced gluconeogenesis by metabolizing glucogenic amino acids, possibly contributing to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis under reduced glucose supply.
evidence: This is a finding supported by metabolomic and biochemical data shown in Figures 3G, 3K, 3L.

claim: Enhanced gluconeogenesis by metabolizing glucogenic amino acids possibly contributes to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis under reduced glucose supply.
source: On the other hand, SE-Low animals showed decreased plasma alanine and alanine aminotransferase activity, and increased levels of blood urea nitrogen, glutamate, and aspartate (Figure 3E, G, J and L), all pointing to the direction of enhanced gluconeogenesis by metabolizing glucogenic amino acids, possibly contributing to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis under reduced glucose supply.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from metabolomic and biochemical data, presented as speculation.

claim: Infection itself dramatically altered the whole blood transcriptome with more than 5000 DEGs.
source: Infection itself dramatically altered the whole blood transcriptome (Figure 4A), with more than 5000 DEGs (all shown in Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Glucose supply in un-infected conditions had limited impact on blood transcriptome.
source: Glucose supply in un-infected conditions had limited impact, while within the infected groups differences in gene expression were much less pronounced than in the liver.
evidence: This is a finding inferred from the transcriptomic analysis comparing groups.

claim: Within the infected groups differences in gene expression were much less pronounced than in the liver.
source: Glucose supply in un-infected conditions had limited impact, while within the infected groups differences in gene expression were much less pronounced than in the liver.
evidence: This is a finding inferred from comparing blood and liver transcriptomic data.

claim: The SE-Low animals showed 321 up-regulated and 363 down-regulated DEGs, compared to SE-High animals in blood.
source: The SE-Low animals showed 321 up-regulated and 363 down-regulated DEGs, compared to SE-High animals.
evidence: This is a finding from the blood transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed a dampened immune response in SE-Low animals.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed a dampened immune response, enhanced glycerolipid metabolic processes, and re-organization of cellular structure in SE-Low animals (Figure 4B-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of blood transcriptomic data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed enhanced glycerolipid metabolic processes in SE-Low animals.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed a dampened immune response, enhanced glycerolipid metabolic processes, and re-organization of cellular structure in SE-Low animals (Figure 4B-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of blood transcriptomic data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed re-organization of cellular structure in SE-Low animals.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis for DEGs between the two infected groups showed a dampened immune response, enhanced glycerolipid metabolic processes, and re-organization of cellular structure in SE-Low animals (Figure 4B-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of blood transcriptomic data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: No enriched pathways related to the metabolism of glucose, fatty acids, or amino acids were observed in blood transcriptome.
source: Surprisingly, no enriched pathways related to the metabolism of glucose, fatty acids, or amino acids were observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis of blood transcriptomic data.

claim: Modulations of hepatic, but not circulating immune cell metabolism, by reduced glucose supply, play a central role in guiding systemic inflammatory responses in preterm neonates.
source: These data strongly suggest that modulations of hepatic, but not circulating immune cell metabolism, by reduced glucose supply, play a central role in guiding systemic inflammatory responses in preterm neonates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined transcriptomic data from liver and blood.

claim: Principal component analysis of proteomic profiles demonstrated no separation among the four groups at 3 hr.
source: Principal component analysis of proteomic profiles (Figure 5A–D) demonstrated no separation among the four groups at 3 hr and marginal separation of SE-High from SE-Low at 6 hr.
evidence: This is a finding supported by PCA of proteomic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Principal component analysis of proteomic profiles demonstrated marginal separation of SE-High from SE-Low at 6 hr.
source: Principal component analysis of proteomic profiles (Figure 5A–D) demonstrated no separation among the four groups at 3 hr and marginal separation of SE-High from SE-Low at 6 hr.
evidence: This is a finding supported by PCA of proteomic data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The full impact of infection and glucose supply on plasma proteome was only obvious at 12 hr and euthanasia.
source: The full impact of infection and glucose supply during infection was only obvious at 12 hr and euthanasia.
evidence: This is a finding supported by PCA of proteomic data shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: Enriched pathways in plasma proteome at 12 hr and euthanasia included immune response, pyruvate metabolism, and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis.
source: We detected similar enriched pathways to other transcriptome/metabolome data at 12 hr and euthanasia: immune response, pyruvate metabolism, and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by pathway enrichment analysis of proteomic data shown in Figures 5E-F.

claim: Levels of proteins encoding for enzyme conversion from pyruvate to lactate (LDHB, DLD) were higher in animals receiving high vs. reduced glucose supply.
source: Specifically, levels of proteins encoding for enzyme conversion from pyruvate to lactate (LDHB, DLD) and upstream conversion of glucose in the glycolysis pathway (ALDOA) were higher in animals receiving high vs. reduced glucose supply, irrespectively of infection status, again showing increased use of glycolysis (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is a finding supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 5G-I (note: text refers to Figure 6G-I but should be 5G-I based on figure numbering).

claim: Levels of ALDOA were higher in animals receiving high vs. reduced glucose supply, irrespectively of infection status.
source: Specifically, levels of proteins encoding for enzyme conversion from pyruvate to lactate (LDHB, DLD) and upstream conversion of glucose in the glycolysis pathway (ALDOA) were higher in animals receiving high vs. reduced glucose supply, irrespectively of infection status, again showing increased use of glycolysis (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is a finding supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 5G-I (note: text refers to Figure 6G-I but should be 5G-I based on figure numbering).

claim: Porcine IAIP components ITIH1 and bikunin were significantly reduced in circulation only under a high PN glucose regimen.
source: Interestingly we observed that porcine IAIP components ITIH1 and bikunin were significantly reduced in circulation only under a high PN glucose regimen.
evidence: This is a finding supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 5J-L.

claim: Levels of heavy chains 1 and 2 as well as an alpha-1-microglobin precursor to Bikunin (AMBP) were significantly higher in SE-Low compared to SE-High.
source: Although, at the end of the experiment, AMBP levels were lower in SE-Low compared to the uninfected group (Figure 5L), levels of heavy chains 1 and 2 as well as an alpha-1-microglobin precursor to Bikunin (AMBP) were significantly higher in SE-Low compared to SE-High, which correlates with a less severe inflammatory response (Figure 5K–L).
evidence: This is a finding supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 5J-L.

claim: No difference in survival could be detected among the three infected groups until 12 hr when glucose was switched at 3 or 6 hr post-infection.
source: No difference in survival could be detected among these three infected groups until 12 hr (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Blood pH gradually dropped and was similar among the groups 3–12 hr post-infection when glucose was switched at 3 or 6 hr.
